conflict_topics: who is responsible for ventilating when cooking (proposed standing rule)
opening the rain-facing window vs protecting Agent C's drying laundry
moving Agent C's drying rack (consent and logistics)
timing and access to the shared stove (Agent A's remaining cooking time vs Agent D's need)
dialogue_quality_notes: Exchanges are concise and task-focused; participants give practical constraints (tutoring, guest, headaches).
Requests and offers converge on a concrete sheltered location (balcony shelf) — pragmatic problem-solving.
No one unilaterally reassigns the drying rack; consent is sought and given conditionally.
evaluation.final_reason: By the end of round 6, the immediate logistics have trended toward agreement (Agent C will move the rack) but the move was not yet completed and the central substantive disputes — whether cooks must accept a standing ventilation rule and who bears ventilation responsibility, plus stove-access timing — remain unsettled.
position_change_notes: Agent C moved from an initial protect-my-belongings stance to agreeing to move the rack if sheltered and quick (explicitly offered in rounds 3 and 5).
Agent B shifted from demanding immediate ventilation to accepting a 15-minute wait with extractor on (round 1) and then pressed for the rack to be moved.
Agent A maintained position of finishing the dish and keeping stove for the promised time while using the extractor; did not concede to stop cooking.
No final change on the standing-rule dispute; stove handover remains pending.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A refuses to stop cooking but turns on extractor and promises 15 minutes; Agent B accepts the 15-minute timeline but the underlying dispute about who must ventilate and a proposed standing rule remains unresolved.

Agent C asserts 'please don't open the window or move my drying rack without asking me'; Agent D asks C to move the rack now so the window will be clear — a clear substantive disagreement over moving C's laundry and opening the window.

Agent B asks C to move the rack; Agent C asks where to put it and offers to move if there's a sheltered spot and it's quick — conflict softens to a logistical question but the move is not yet completed.
Agent B and D propose the balcony shelf by the fridge as a sheltered spot; no rejection from C yet, the issue remains logistical and unresolved until moved.

Agent A asks C to move the rack now; Agent C agrees and says it will take ~2 minutes and requests the window remain closed until then — the immediate movement issue reaches agreement but broader disputes (ventilation responsibility/rule, stove access timing) remain unsettled.

Agent D checks if C moved the rack; C says not yet but can move now and asks again that the window remain closed until it's on the shelf. Cooperative but the move is pending and core issues (who must ventilate, standing rule, stove handover) remain unresolved.

substantive_insights: Tension is primarily practical: balancing immediate cooking needs and odour mitigation against preserving another's belongings (laundry) from rain.
Agents articulate clear, competing constraints (Agent B's headaches; Agent C's tutoring schedule and risk of wet laundry; Agent A's commitment to a guest), which shapes willingness to compromise.
Agreement on logistics (where to move the rack) reduces acute conflict, but normative disagreement about long-term responsibility for ventilation remains unresolved.
